intended_object: The family (X, Y) of two objects, indexed by the two-element set {left, right} (`WalkingPair`): it sends left to X and right to Y. This comes from the docstring and from how it is used to turn binary (bi)cones into (bi)cones over a family of objects.
explanation:
The body uses `WalkingPair.casesOn j X Y`, which sends `left` to `X` and `right` to `Y`. That is exactly the indexed pair the docstring describes, and the simp lemmas `pairFunction_left` and `pairFunction_right` confirm it. The definition needs nothing from `C`: it is just a type, with no category structure assumed, so the generality is already as wide as it can be. In Mathlib it serves as the object part of the binary family. Downstream code uses it to relate binary biproducts to biproducts over `WalkingPair`, and to build sieves from two arrows. Nothing is missing or wrong.

The closest other Mathlib construction is `![X, Y]`, a family indexed by `Fin 2`. It uses a different index type, so it is not the same declaration, and I give no `mathlib_counterpart`. The verdict is faithful.
